topic.title: What if all of Antarctica's ice melted?
topic.map_answer: new coastlines drawn on the world map: the sea moving inland over the low places (the Netherlands, Bangladesh, Florida) as Antarctica's ice turns to water

title: What if Antarctica's ice all melted?
description:
What if every bit of ice on Antarctica melted away?
Antarctica, the Netherlands, Bangladesh and Florida, with the new coastlines on the map, as a thought experiment.
Sources: National Snow and Ice Data Center (Jan 2024). The characters are not advisers.
Maps simplified. Borders as recognised by the country each video is about.
cta: Netherlands or Florida: which new coastline surprised you more? Comment

lines.text: Antarctica's ice melts, all of it. Which countries vanish from the map first?
From space, Antarctica is a whole white continent at the bottom of the world, buried under ice so thick it hides whole mountain ranges.
Melt it, and all that water runs into the one ocean that touches every coast on Earth. So where does it hit first?
Start in Europe. The Netherlands is low, flat land, and the North Sea pours in until most of it is gone, Amsterdam and Rotterdam included.
Fly east to Bangladesh, a country of river mouths. Most of it slips under the Bay of Bengal, and the capital, Dhaka, goes with it.
Across the Atlantic, the sea closes in on Florida's long peninsula, and most of the state is under water too.
But those three keep their high ground. So which countries lose everything?
Out in the Indian Ocean lie the Maldives, hundreds of coral islands, none much higher than a house. Every one goes under. A whole country, gone.
Then the Pacific: Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands, whole nations built on low rings of coral, wiped off the map.
All because the sea would stand about 58 m higher than it does today, and their highest ground is nowhere near that.
Netherlands or Florida: which new coastline surprised you more? Tell me below, before Antarctica's ice melts, all of it.

Re-review of 3 extended lines: Amsterdam (about -2 to +2 m) and Rotterdam (much of it below sea level, lowest about -6 m) and Dhaka (about 4-15 m above sea level, Britannica/World Bank range) all lie far below a 58 m rise (NSIDC), so 'Amsterdam and Rotterdam included' and 'Dhaka goes with it' are true; water line adds only a question. Earlier checks stand.

Round 3: every beat is directed on the map (11 places). The water now visibly fills the Netherlands, Bangladesh and Florida. The payoff's 58 m sign stands on a gauge at the Maldives, with no box and clear of the captions. The first frame names Antarctica, the loop returns to it, and the closing question is a pick-one. 64 s, layout clean, audio -1/-15.9 dB, disclaimer in the description.

facts[0] / payoff beat ('about {fact1}' = 60 m): the cited source (nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/ice-sheets, fetched 2026-11-21) says 'If the entire Antarctic Ice Sheet melted, sea level would rise about 58 meters (190 feet)'. Value 60 does not match the source; web search also gives 58 m (Al Jazeera 57 m), no source found for 60. Fix: set the fact value to 58 (unit m, NSIDC) in topics.json and script.json; the line 'about fifty-eight metres' then stands.

Note for the rewrite (not a separate failure): florida beat/moment 'only a thin strip in the north is left' is loose: at ~58 m most of the peninsula goes, but the high central ridge (to ~95 m) and parts of the panhandle stay. 'most of the state is under water' is right; consider 'shrinks to its northern hills and a few ridge islands' or keep the line vague. Rest checked and fine: ice beat (new line, no Europe claim; hidden mountain ranges e.g. Gamburtsev true), Netherlands/Bangladesh mostly below 58 m, Maldives (highest ~2.4 m), Tuvalu (~4.6 m), Marshall Islands (~10 m); description ends with the channel disclaimer; no advice, tone fine.

[script] 55.0s payoff (beat payoff, place 'the world with its new coastlines, a sea gauge at the Maldives'): the world map is buried under one big flat translucent blue rectangle with a ruler down the middle and a '58 m' signboard; no new coastline and no Maldives are visible, so the payoff is a slide over a dimmed map rather than the answer drawn on the map (lesson 1). Show the flooded coastlines (Netherlands, Bangladesh, Florida gone, the island nations gone), with the gauge standing on the Maldives.

[script] 20.0s dutch and 25.0s bengal: the Netherlands is lit orange (with a tangle of overlapping windmills) and Bangladesh is lit green with a flag. Neither shows the sea coming in, though the lines say 'the North Sea pours in until most of it is gone' and 'most of it slips under the Bay of Bengal'. Only Florida (35.0s) is drawn under water. The flood is the video's whole answer, so each of these beats needs the water to fill the land on its words ('pours', 'slips under').

[scene] 40.0s maldives (component Maldives): the Maldives islands are drawn as a single vertical stack of palm-tree islands sitting on top of each other, which looks like a glitch. At 45.0s the 'HOUSE' label sits right on top of the 'MALDIVES' label, and the house and gauge float in a hard-edged translucent rectangle that is off to the side of the islands. Spread the atolls down their real chain, put the house and gauge on one island, and keep the labels apart.
